content: Observational studies have indicated a link between transiently low thyroid hormone levels in preterm infants during the first weeks of life, a condition known as transient hypothyroxinemia, and abnormal neurodevelopmental outcomes. It has been hypothesized that thyroid hormone therapy could potentially prevent these adverse outcomes. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether administering thyroid hormone therapy to preterm infants without congenital hypothyroidism leads to significant changes in neonatal and long-term outcomes, both in terms of benefits and potential harms. The review employed the standard search strategy of the Neonatal Review Group, which included comprehensive searches of databases such as the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, and MEDLINE. It also incorporated data from previous reviews, cross-references, conference proceedings, expert informants, and handsearching of relevant journals. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized or quasi-randomized trials that compared thyroid hormone therapy (either as treatment or prophylaxis) to a control group in preterm infants. The primary clinical outcomes assessed were neurodevelopmental outcomes and mortality. The quality of the trials was evaluated, and data were extracted and synthesized using standard Cochrane Collaboration methods, including relative risk (RR) and weighted mean difference (WMD) calculations. Nine studies were identified that compared thyroid hormone treatment to a control group. Of these, four were randomized trials (Chowdhry 1984, van Wassenaer 1997, Vanhole 1997, Smith 2000), and one was a quasi-randomized trial (Amato 1989). All studies included preterm infants born at less than 32 weeks of gestation, but the timing, dose, and duration of thyroid hormone treatment varied across studies. Four studies used thyroxine, while one (Amato 1989) used triiodothyronine. Only two studies (van Wassenaer 1997, Vanhole 1997) had robust methodologies for neurodevelopmental follow-up. The studies were generally small in size, with the largest (van Wassenaer 1997) enrolling 200 infants. A meta-analysis of five studies found no significant difference in mortality rates at discharge between infants who received thyroid hormone treatment and those in the control group (typical RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.17). A meta-analysis of two studies (van Wassenaer 1997, Vanhole 1997) found no significant differences in neurodevelopmental outcomes, as measured by the Bayley Mental Development Index (MDI) or Psychomotor Development Index (PDI) at 7-12 months. Similarly, van Wassenaer 1997 reported no significant differences in the Bayley MDI and PDI at 24 months, the incidence of cerebral palsy (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.84), combined death and cerebral palsy rates (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.14), or the RAKIT IQ score (WMD -2.10, 95% CI -7.91 to 3.71) at 5-7 years of age. One small quasi-randomized study found that the fraction of inspired oxygen was lower in infants receiving triiodothyronine, but this effect was not observed in infants receiving thyroxine in a randomized study. Additionally, early thyroid hormone therapy did not reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation or the incidence of chronic lung disease. The authors concluded that the current evidence does not support the use of thyroid hormones in preterm infants to reduce neonatal mortality, improve neurodevelopmental outcomes, or decrease the severity of respiratory distress syndrome. An analysis of data from one study (van Wassenaer 1997) suggested potential benefits in infants born at 24-25 weeks of gestation, but this finding was not prespecified and should be interpreted with caution. The small sample sizes of the included studies limit the statistical power of the meta-analysis to detect clinically significant differences in neonatal outcomes. The authors recommend that future trials should be adequately powered to detect meaningful differences in neurodevelopmental outcomes. These trials should focus on enrolling infants who are most likely to benefit from thyroid hormone therapy, such as those born at less than 27 weeks of gestation.
